summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 so a mobile node may register several care-of addresses at once with its home agent and correspondents, instead of just one primary address, for reasons like cost, bandwidth and delay.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC extends Mobile IPv6 so one mobile node can register several care-of addresses for one home address. A binding identifier lets the node and its home agent manage each address separately.

questions: what is multiple care-of addresses registration
what is a binding identifier in mobile ipv6
what is bulk registration in mobile ipv6
subtitle: Mobile IPv6 can register several care-of addresses and manage each binding with an identifier.

tldr.problem: Base Mobile IPv6 allowed only one care-of address to be registered for a home address, even when a mobile node had several active network connections.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node assigns each binding a 16-bit Binding Identification number and carries it in a new mobility option. A home agent stores a separate binding for each identifier.
tldr.outcome: A node can register and update several care-of addresses, including in one bulk update to its home agent. RFC 5648 is updated by RFC 6089.

today: RFC 5648 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2009, and is updated by RFC 6089. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: One Home Address, Multiple Connections
sections.content:
A mobile node may have several network interfaces or several global addresses on one interface. Base Mobile IPv6 allowed it to register only one care-of address at a time for its home address, preventing simultaneous use of those connections with Mobile IPv6 session continuity.

RFC 5648 extends Mobile IPv6 to register multiple care-of addresses with a home agent and correspondent nodes. The same binding-management mechanism can also be used by mobile routers following the NEMO Basic Support protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node can have several active network addresses. This extension lets it register more than one address for its home address.

sections.title: Binding Identifiers and Binding Entries
sections.content:
The mobile node assigns a Binding Identification number (BID) to each care-of address. A BID is a 16-bit unsigned integer; zero is reserved, and BIDs for one home address must be unique at the same time. The node stores each BID in its Binding Update List.

A home agent copies the BID into the corresponding binding-cache entry. If it receives a BID that does not match an existing entry, it creates a new entry. When a receiver does not support the extension, it can ignore the unknown option and process the update using base Mobile IPv6 rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Each registered address has its own identifier. The receiver uses that identifier to find or create the matching binding entry.

sections.title: The Binding Identifier Option
sections.content:
The Binding Identifier mobility option carries the BID, a status field, an H flag, and an optional care-of address. Its type is 35. Its length is 4 when no address is present, 8 for an IPv4 address, or 20 for an IPv6 address.

The Binding Update also gains an Overwrite (O) flag. When set, the receiver replaces the mobile node's existing bindings with the bindings in that update. The option can appear in Binding Updates, Binding Acknowledgements, Binding Refresh Requests, and Care-of Test messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The option identifies one binding and can carry its address and status. The update's O flag says whether the receiver should replace its existing bindings.

sections.title: Registering, Updating, and Removing Bindings
sections.content:
For a first registration of a BID, the mobile node MUST include the care-of address. Later refreshes and removals can identify the binding by BID alone. A lifetime of zero removes the specified BID; a zero-lifetime update without the option removes all bindings.

Bulk registration puts several Binding Identifier options in one Binding Update and is allowed only for home registration, not registration with a correspondent node. When a node first registers after startup, it MUST set the O flag because it may not know which older entries remain at the home agent. One packet flow SHOULD use only one care-of address at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can update or remove one binding by naming its identifier. It can send several bindings to its home agent in one update, but not bulk-register them with a correspondent node.

sections.title: Home-Agent Processing and Returning Home
sections.content:
The home agent searches for a binding using the home address and BID when the BID is known. It updates an existing matching entry or creates a new one. If part of a bulk registration fails, the acknowledgement can report a status for each BID and use MCOA NOTCOMPLETE for the overall result.

A mobile node may remain connected to both its home link and foreign links. The home agent must intercept traffic and select a route. If other routers share the home link, the mobile node MUST NOT use Neighbor Discovery for its home address there; the acknowledgement reports MCOA RETURNHOME WO/NDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent keeps a separate entry for each identifier and can report which registrations failed. When a node uses home and foreign links together, the home agent and node must avoid competing to answer for the home address.

sections.title: IPsec and Address-Redirection Risk
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 uses IPsec to protect signaling, and RFC 5648 describes how multiple care-of addresses interact with IPsec and IKEv2. For each home address, the node chooses one care-of address for IKEv2 messages; it can change that address through a Binding Update with the K flag or re-establish the security association.

A malicious mobile node could claim victims' addresses as care-of addresses and cause its home agent to tunnel traffic to them. The RFC advises home agents to verify care-of addresses before using them, but leaves the verification method out of scope. Bulk registration cannot perform the usual reachability check, so a home agent may reject it.
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple bindings increase the risk that a node will claim an address it does not control. A home agent should verify addresses before using them as destinations for tunneled traffic.
